facts.text: Polymetallic nodules are potato-sized lumps rich in nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese that lie on the deep seabed.
The nodules typically lie more than three kilometres below the surface, for example in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone of the Pacific.
Electric car batteries need metals such as cobalt, nickel and manganese.
Most of these metals now come from mines on land, which have been linked to deforestation, water pollution and human rights abuses.
Nodules form over millions of years.
Deep-sea life is poorly known; surveys of nodule fields keep finding new species, and millions of species may still be undescribed.
Tracks ploughed into the Peru Basin seabed in a 1989 experiment were still visible decades later, and fewer microbes, worms and sea cucumbers lived in them.
Mining would release clouds of sediment-laden water that could harm filter-feeding animals.
Pacific tuna fisheries overlap with deep-sea mining exploration areas, and waste released in midwater could disturb the food webs that tuna depend on.
Some battery types, such as lithium iron phosphate batteries, contain no cobalt or nickel.
Recycling old batteries is expected to supply a growing share of battery metals in the coming decades.
